text: Controllers in ASP .NET Core Web API

What are Controllers? • In ASP.NET Core Web API, controllers are responsible for handling HTTP requests and returning data (usually in JSON or XML format) to the client. • They manage the flow of data between the server and the client. • Roles of Controller: – Request Handling: Controllers receive HTTP requests and send responses. – Data Processing: They interact with models to process data and implement application logic. – Response Generation: Controllers decide the type of response sent back
plement application logic. – Response Generation: Controllers decide the type of response sent back to the client, whether it’s data, status codes, error messages, etc

Adding Controller Class • The Controller class in ASP.NET Core Web API must have the “Controller” suffix. • For example, if developer wants to add a controller with the name Home, then the name should be HomeController. • Controllers in ASP.NET Core Web API are typically created by inheriting from the ControllerBase class. – This provides access to several helper methods and properties that are useful for handling HTTP requests and responses.

Adding Controller Class • API Controller – Empty: • This template creates a basic API controller class without any predefined actions. • It’s suitable when developer wants full control over defining own actions and routing. • Developer needs to use this template when it is preferred to manually define all CRUD operations and their corresponding HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE). • It starts with an empty controller class that needs to be populated with the desired actions.

Adding Controller Class • API Controller with Read/Write Actions: • This template scaffolds a controller with basic CRUD actions (Get, Post, Put, Delete). • It’s useful for quickly setting up a controller that supports standard RESTful operations. • It sets up actions for listing all resources, retrieving a resource by ID, creating a new resource, updating an existing resource, and deleting a resource.

Adding Controller Class • API Controller with Actions using Entity Framework: • This template extends the “API Controller with Read/Write Actions” template by integrating with Entity Framework Core. • It includes actions that interact with a database using EF Core for data access operations. • It sets up actions that use EF Core to perform CRUD operations on database entities.

Adding Controller Class • API with Read/Write Endpoints: • Similar to “API Controller with Read/Write Actions,” this template includes actions for CRUD operations but provides more flexibility in customizing endpoint names and HTTP verbs. • This template should be used when it is needed to have more control over endpoint naming or to include additional actions beyond basic CRUD operations.

Adding Controller Class • API Controller with Read/Write Endpoints using Entity Framework: • This template Combines the features of “API Controller with Actions using Entity Framework” with the flexibility of customized endpoint names and HTTP verbs. • Developer needs to choose this template when it is required to have both database integration (via EF Core) and custom endpoint naming.

Features of Controllers • Controllers use attributes to define routes. • The [Route] attribute specifies how to access the controller via URL patterns. • The [ApiController] attribute decorates the class to enable Web API-specific behaviors. • Inside controllers, methods known as action methods respond to HTTP requests. • Each method is typically decorated with an attribute corresponding to an HTTP method ([HttpGet], [HttpPost], etc.), defining what type of request it handles.

Features of Controllers • Action methods can accept parameters directly from the route, query string or body of the request, which ASP.NET Core binds automatically. • Controllers use IActionResult or ActionResult<T> to return responses. • These can encapsulate various HTTP responses, allowing for easy customization of status codes and payloads.

Features of APIController Attribute • Automatic HTTP 400 Responses: • When applied to a controller, ASP.NET Core automatically validates the model state of incoming HTTP requests. • Attribute Routing Requirement: • The [ApiController] attribute makes attribute routing mandatory for the controller. • This means developer must use [Route], [HttpGet], [HttpPost], etc., to define routes for the controller’s actions.
ller’s actions.

Features of APIController Attribute • Binding Source Parameter Inference: • The [ApiController] attribute enhances the binding of incoming data by inferring where to look for data based on the type of the parameter and the HTTP method of the request. • For example, in case of a POST method, it assumes binding from the request body. • Problem Details for HTTP Error Responses: • When an action method returns an error (e.g., BadRequest, NotFound, Internal Server Error), the [ApiController] attribut
d returns an error (e.g., BadRequest, NotFound, Internal Server Error), the [ApiController] attribute automatically generates a ProblemDetails response

Choosing between Controller and ControllerBase Classes • APIs: • For building a RESTful API without views, ControllerBase is used to keep the project lightweight and focused on data endpoints. • MVC Applications: • If the application requires server-side rendering of views using Razor views, Controller is used to leverage its support for views and related functionalities.
